Excitingly interesting to see what asteroid mining will do to notions of scarcity. This is just one asteroid among many thousands if not millions in our near to relatively near vicinity. And this is near future stuff. We've already managed to land and return multiple missions from asteroids. It's just a matter of increasing the scale and robustness.

I also wonder how companies will approach monetizing the materials on Earth. To say this would flood the market is an understatement.
Near future stuff if we can keep from 1984ing.

It's still expensive as hell to send anything into space, let alone up, mine shit, and come back (even though lower gravity on asteroids makes "coming back" less of an issue fuel-wise). We also can't just drag asteroids into Earth to mine at our convenience without most of it burning up in the atmosphere or causing catastrophic damage to everything, depending on the size of the asteroid. Unless we figure out a way around one of those problems, materials that could be mined from space aren't going to affect the market too much for the time being.

Not really, relative to the scale of money involved here. For instance let's take technology that is in no way geared towards something like this - the SpaceX Dragon storage capsule. That launches on a Falcon 9 and costs about $60 million. It has a return payload of 3,000kg. At current prices, that's $120million of gold. The efficiency there could be improved substantially as the primary purpose of the vessel is to launch things into space - not to return them. That's also just gold. Platinum is actually worth substantially more per pound and just as abundant. Getting the ore from orbit back to Earth is no economic problem. The only major cost issue is how much would it cost to have a reusable tanker bring ore from an asteroid to Earth's orbit. I can't imagine any sort of number you could put there that would be realistic and constraining to the potential of this.
I think building a huge tanker is a waste. Building a barge and tugging whole asteroid seems like a better use of the resources!

Two points, one for and one against.

For: That $60mil for a Dragon launch is to get it up into orbit, and there are companies lined up to pay that. There's not much that comes back from space yet, so if someone else has already paid to get the capsule up there, that 3 tons of return cargo is effectively almost free.

Against: That's only going to low Earth orbit, the asteroids are a LOT further away than that (in fact, they're somewhere between Mars and Jupiter in terms of difference).

The idea would be to have at least two vessels. One is carrying ore back and forth from the asteroid, the other is launching things into space that the ore is loaded into and brought back into earth on, like the Dragon. Presumably that step is also where the tanker would be refueled. Something like 95% of a rocket's cargo when blasting off from Earth is going to be fuel and that storage volume is generally separated during ascent just to reach that level of 'efficiency'. Makes a lot more sense to have a dedicated space-only transit vehicle vehicle rather than having one super-vehicle that does everything. Might even make more sense to also have smaller launch vessels on the asteroid as well.

In addition, once you get to the asteroid belt, even taking into account that the asteroids are incredibly far apart from eachother, there are either other asteroids or the same asteroid has the ingredients to make rocket fuel. So your refueling is trivial once you get out there the first time (or three).
